rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L01.html Theorem 6.4 (Ville) and proof, lines 281-294 [8d2fca9 numbering]
rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: Re-derived step by step. B_k = {M_j < h for all j <= k}, B_{−1} = Ω, A_k = B_{k−1} \ B_k; the A_k are disjoint, their union is {max_{k<=n} M_k >= h}, and A_k, B_k are functions of Y_1..Y_k. For W_n = Σ_{k<=n} M_k·1_{A_k} + M_n·1_{B_n}, A_n ∪ B_n = B_{n−1} (disjoint) gives W_n − W_{n−1} = (M_n − M_{n−1})·1_{B_{n−1}}. Taking out what is known gives E_0[W_n − W_{n−1}] = E_0[1_{B_{n−1}}(E_0[M_n|past] − M_{n−1})] <= 0, with integrability from E_0[M_t] <= 1, and W_0 = M_0 = 1. W_n >= h·1{max >= h}, so P(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) <= 1/h; then continuity from below; then the h' < h argument extends the bound to {sup >= h}. Complete, and it needs no optional-stopping theorem (M6). The supermartingale version generalizes the cited test-martingale Eq. (8) and is proved on the page. rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: Re-derived from scratch (line 440 changed). With A_n the event that some look among the first n rejects (Proposition 6.1), A_n is contained in A_{n+1}, so an added look can only add rejections, with extra probability P(A_{n+1} minus A_n). For normal data that difference contains the open set {|S_t| < b_t for t <= n, |S_{n+1}| > b_{n+1}} for any finite positive boundaries b_t: it is nonempty (y_1 = ... = y_n = 0, y_{n+1} = 2 b_{n+1}) and the density of (Y_1, ..., Y_{n+1}) is positive everywhere, so the probability is positive. A design whose rejection probability already equals alpha (all of alpha spent) therefore exceeds alpha when the look is added. The paragraph states the qualifiers 'for normal data' and 'a design that has spent all of alpha'. rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: (a) Independence under every null distribution gives E_0[∏E_i] = ∏E_0[E_i] <= 1. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L01.html Lab 4 interpretation, line 422, the derivation after the T span [8d2fca9 numbering]
rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: New displayed result since 9b6be31, re-derived. Claim: with h = 1/alpha, h P0(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) + E0[sum_{k<=n} (M_k - h) 1_{A_k}] <= 1. Derivation: Theorem 6.4's proof gives E0[W_n] <= 1 with W_n = sum_k M_k 1_{A_k} + M_n 1_{B_n}; drop the nonnegative term M_n 1_{B_n} and write M_k = h + (M_k - h) on A_k. Sound. Second claim: the expected overshoot O_n = E0[sum_{k<=n}(M_k - h) 1_{A_k}] is nondecreasing in n because every summand is >= 0 (M_k >= h on A_k); it is positive from the first day n_0 with P(A_{n_0}) > 0 because M_{n_0} > h almost surely on A_{n_0} (shown in the previous sentence for the monitor); so P(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) <= (1 - O_n)/h = alpha (1 - O_n) <= alpha (1 - O_{n_0}) for n >= n_0, and letting n grow (monotone limit) the probability of ever crossing is at most alpha (1 - O_{n_0}) < alpha. Sound; for this monitor n_0 = 1 and the gap is tiny in absolute terms but strictly positive, and the sentence claims only 'strictly below alpha'. Numerical spot-check (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify8-L01-L02/overshoot.py, 40,000 null paths of the monitor with alpha = 0.05, kappa = 252, horizon 2520): P(cross) = 0.0199 < 0.05, E[overshoot] = 0.0191 > 0, h P + O = 0.417 <= E[W_n] = 0.989 <= 1. Notation: h, M_k, A_k, B_k and 'the same steps' refer to the proof of Theorem 6.4, which the sentence names; A_n of Proposition 6.1's proof is a different, proof-local event, so there is no collision inside either proof. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'Set-up' and 'Construction' (lines 437-440)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: Re-derived. m' = m - i + 1 true nulls, c = min(c_i, 1/m'). Since alpha < 1 and c_i > alpha/m' we have c > alpha/m' (both c_i and 1/m' exceed alpha/m'), so m'c > alpha. Construction: i - 1 false nulls at p-value 0 (a false null's p-value is unconstrained; validity is required only of true nulls), true nulls q_j = (U + (j-1)/m') mod 1 for U uniform on [0,1): each q_j is uniform (rotation of the circle), hence valid (P(q_j <= u) = u). Assumptions complete: alpha in (0,1), positive constants, any other constants. The device is the one of Problem P2 (p_2 = (U + 1/2) mod 1), as the page says. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'A false rejection' (lines 443-445)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: Re-derived. Almost surely every q_j > 0 (q_j = 0 only for one value of U), so the i - 1 zeros are p_(1) = ... = p_(i-1) = 0 and p_(i) = min_j q_j belongs to a true null. Zeros pass steps 1, ..., i - 1 because the constants are positive (the step fails only when p_(k) > c_k). If min_j q_j <= c <= c_i, step i passes, so the first failing index is > i and H_(i), a true null, is rejected. Hence FWER >= P(min q <= c) = m'c = min(m' c_i, 1) > alpha (m' c_i > alpha by hypothesis, 1 > alpha). The page states it as an inequality; the equality FWER = min(m' c_i, 1) also holds (step i is then decisive: it passes iff min q <= c_i, and the arcs of length c_i cover the circle when c_i >= 1/m'), which I confirmed numerically; the lesson does not need it. [git diff 202ea24..50d202e changes course/modules/S/S7/L02.html at line 88 only (the fwer-growth caption); the passage of this row is outside that line.]

rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: Re-derived. False-null p-values in (0, delta] with delta <= c_j for all j < i: on {delta < min_j q_j <= c} the i - 1 smallest p-values are the false nulls' (each <= delta <= its constant, so steps 1..i-1 pass) and p_(i) = min q <= c <= c_i passes, so a true null is rejected. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'What it shows' (line 449)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: Checked sentence by sentence. (1) 'A step-down procedure with fixed constants that controls the FWER at level alpha under every joint distribution of valid p-values must have c_k <= alpha/(m + 1 - k) for every k': the contrapositive of the main result (positive constants, alpha < 1). (2) 'Raising constants only adds rejections, because the first failure moves later, so Holm's procedure rejects everything such a procedure rejects, for every vector of p-values': if c_k <= Holm_k for all k then p_(k) > Holm_k implies p_(k) > c_k, so the first failing index of the c-procedure is no later than Holm's and it rejects a subset. (3) 'A gain beyond Holm's needs the dependence between the tests (Lessons 4 and 5)': true for the class the problem treats (p-value step-down with fixed constants, every configuration of true nulls possible, only marginal validity). Outside that class gains can come from logical relations between the hypotheses (Shaffer 1986) as well as from dependence; the sentence is a pointer, sits after the sentence that fixes the class, and is not a graded claim span. Note, not a failure. (4) The T span after it matches Lehmann and Romano Theorem 2.3(ii) (L02-cite-lehmann2005generalizations). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 88 (new figcaption sentence)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: New sentence: 'testing each hypothesis at α/m holds the family-wise error rate at or below α for every m, and here, with independent nulls, at exactly α only when m = 1.' Derivation: by Boole's inequality (as in the proof of Theorem 2.2), the FWER of m true nulls each tested at α/m is at most m·(α/m) = α for any dependence, so 'at or below α for every m' holds. With independent true nulls, FWER = 1 − (1 − α/m)^m. Bernoulli's inequality (1 − x)^m ≥ 1 − mx holds with strict inequality for m ≥ 2 and 0 < x < 1, so FWER < α for m ≥ 2; at m = 1 the FWER is exactly α. Numerical check (scratch scripts/card_numbers.py, python -I, .venv): for α = 0.01..0.10 and m = 1..200, 500, 1000, 5000: 0 violations of FWER ≤ α; strictly below α for every m ≥ 2; |FWER − α| ≤ 1e-15 at m = 1. Values: α = 0.05: FWER(2) = 0.049375, FWER(1000) = 0.048772; α = 0.01: FWER(1000) = 0.009950. The figure's readout and desc in every state agree (row L02-fig-fwer-growth). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P2 solution, line 421, the shifted construction
rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: Re-derived at 535fd80 with s = alpha/2 and p2 = (U + s) mod 1. For U in [0, 1 - s): p2 = U + s > s, so p2 <= s only at U = 0 (p2 = s). For U in [1 - s, 1): p2 = U + s - 1 in [0, s), so p2 <= s. Hence {p2 <= s} = {0} u [1 - s, 1) (exact on the 160000-point rational grid: p2_recheck_535fd80.out section 2, 'A2 equals {0} u [1 - alpha/2, 1) on the grid: True'). Since s < 1 - s for alpha < 1, {U <= s} n {p2 <= s} = {0}, a null set. P(A1) = P(A2) = s, P(A1 n A2) = 0, so P(union) = 2s = alpha. The text 'which meets {U <= alpha/2} only at the null point U = 0, so the two events are disjoint up to a null set and the FWER is again exactly alpha' is TRUE. Monte Carlo: section 3 (mean over 20 seeds of 1,000,000 draws: 0.050002 +- 0.000035). Round-15 FAIL (L02-math-P2-shift-disjoint PASS in round 15) re-checked and still PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P2 solution, line 421 ('E[U((U+s) mod 1)] = 1/3 - s(1-s)/2 ... correlation 1 - 6s(1-s)')
rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: Derivation at 535fd80. V = (U + s) mod 1 equals U + s on [0, 1-s) and U + s - 1 on [1-s, 1]. E[UV] = int_0^{1-s} u(u+s) du + int_{1-s}^1 u(u+s-1) du = [(1-s)^3/3 + s(1-s)^2/2] + [1/3 - (1-s)/2 + (1-s)^3/6] = (1-s)^2/2 + 1/3 - (1-s)/2 = 1/3 - s(1-s)/2 (using (1-s)^3/2 + s(1-s)^2/2 = (1-s)^2/2 and (1-s)^2/2 - (1-s)/2 = -s(1-s)/2). With E U = E V = 1/2 and Var U = Var V = 1/12 (V uniform), Cov = 1/12 - s(1-s)/2 and corr = 12 Cov = 1 - 6s(1-s). Numerical check: p2_recheck_535fd80.out section 1 evaluates both identities with Fraction arithmetic at 28 rational shifts (k/13, k/97, 1/2, 1/40, 1/20, 1/10, 3/7, 1/4, 2/9, 7/11): both hold exactly at every point (printed: 'points tested: 28'). E[UV] and corr are polynomials of degree at most 3 in s, so 28 exact agreements cover the family. PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 129 (the paragraph after Example 2.4), first sentence: 'The bound in (1) is attained when the true-null p-values are uniform and their rejection events {p_i <= alpha/m} are pairwise disjoint up to a null set (Problem P2)'
rows.evidence: unchanged since 00e22e4 (git diff checked); round-21 evidence: Re-checked at 45fff85 (line 129 changed: 'disjoint' became 'disjoint up to a null set'). Proof: P(union A_i) = sum_i P(A_i minus union_{j<i} A_j), and P(A_i minus ...) = P(A_i) iff P(A_i and A_j) = 0 for every j < i; so Boole's inequality is an equality iff the pairwise intersections are null (the 'up to a null set' qualifier is exactly right). With uniform true-null p-values, P(p_i <= alpha/m) = alpha/m, so FWER = m0 alpha/m. Construction (P2, exact check p2_p4_exact.out): p1 = U, p2 = (U + alpha/2) mod 1 gives P(A) = P(B) = alpha/2, P(A and B) = 0 and P(A or B) = alpha exactly (alpha = 1/20). Sufficiency is shown; the sentence's 'attained when' is a sufficient condition, which is what it claims.

(1) OpenCitations index v2, no key: https://api.opencitations.net/index/v2/citations/doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2005.00615.x -> 711 citation rows, 708 distinct citing DOIs, creation years 2004-2026 (oc_citations_romano.json; citing_dois.json). (18 requests, 2 s apart, no identifying parameter): 707 of 708 returned (the missing 10.4225/03/5935ff87c8d5c is not a Crossref DOI). (3) Keyword screen on title or abstract (power, stepwise, step-down, familywise, FWER, multiple testing, data snooping, bootstrap, Holm, Bonferroni, single-step, dependen*): 164 hits, 108 with an abstract (keyword_hits.json). Read in full (abstracts): 10.1093/jjfinec/nbaf020 (Bouamara, Laurent & Shi 2025, StepC): 'more powerful than conventional multiple testing corrections' is a competitor's claim, not a contest of the comparison. 10.1111/jofi.12951 (Harvey & Liu 2020, JF): 'Evaluating current methods, we find that they lack power to detect outperforming managers': an absolute-power finding in fund selection, which does not compare stepwise with single-step methods. 10.1093/rapstu/raaa003 (2020, evaluation of multiple testing methods in finance): simulation comparison of methods; its abstract states no contest of this comparison (body not reachable). 10.1177/1536867x20976314 (Clarke, Romano & Wolf 2020, Stata): 'This correction is considerably more powerful than earlier multiple-testing procedures, such as the Bonferroni and Holm corrections': supports the claim. 10.1093/rfs/hhaa111 (Thousands of Alpha Tests, 2020) and 10.1093/rfs/hhaa018 (Anomalies and False Rejections, 2020): no stepwise comparison. 10.1214/009053607000000550 and 10.1214/009053606000000461 (k-FWER step-up, 2006-2008): no contest. (4) Dey (2024), 'On limiting behaviors of stepwise multiple testing procedures', Statistical Papers, doi 10.1007/s00362-024-01613-6 (not in the citing list; Crossref abstract read): 'under the multivariate normal setups with some correlation structures, the probability of rejecting one or more null hypotheses approaches zero asymptotically for any step-down procedure ... the FWER and power of the step-down procedures also tend to be asymptotically zero'. This is a limit in the number of hypotheses under positive equicorrelation for every step-down procedure, and Bonferroni's power goes to zero there too; it does not compare stepwise with single-step methods, so it does not contest 'often rejects more false hypotheses than single-step methods' at finite m. Recorded as a scope note (freshness_flags). Result: no named published source contests the comparative claim; per VERIFIER_RULES 2.3 this row passes. Crossref and OpenCitations only; OpenAlex not used.

(1) Publisher record: Crossref 10.1111/j.1468-0262.2005.00615.x (curl, no identifying parameter; scratch downloads/romano/crossref_romano.json): 'Stepwise Multiple Testing as Formalized Data Snooping', Econometrica 73(4) 1237-1282, July 2005 (= registry). (2) Published abstract: the Econometric Society page for the article (https://www.econometricsociety.org/publications/econometrica/2005/07/01/stepwise-multiple-testing-formalized-data-snooping, HTTP 200; scratch downloads/romano/es_romano.html), quoted: 'This paper suggests a stepwise multiple testing procedure that asymptotically controls the familywise error rate. Compared to related single-step methods, the procedure is more powerful and often will reject more false hypotheses. ... Unlike some stepwise methods, the method implicitly captures the joint dependence structure of the test statistics ...'. IDEAS (scratch downloads/romano/ideas_romano.html, meta description, 'Copyright The Econometric Society 2005') gives the same sentences. (3) Author copy of the published article (M. Wolf's UZH publications page links etca.pdf; 46 pp.; header 'Econometrica, Vol. 73, No. 4 (July, 2005), 1237-1282'; text at scratch downloads/romano/romano_wolf_2005_etca.txt): keywords 'Bootstrap, data snooping, familywise error, multiple testing, stepwise method'; Algorithm 3.2 computes the critical values 'via the bootstrap'; Theorem 3.1(ii): 'The method asymptotically controls the FWE at level alpha; that is, lim_T FWEP <= alpha'; Section 3 (p. 1246): 'The stepwise procedure is therefore more powerful than the single-step method. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 345 (section 5, bullet 2: the bold headline 'FWER is the wrong target when discoveries are many.' and the sentence that attributes a hedged position to Harvey, Liu and Zhu)
rows.evidence: The bold headline is an unhedged claim of the page's own. Its only grade is the B span on the next sentence, which attributes to Harvey, Liu and Zhu the hedged position: 'when the total number of discoveries is large, one or even a few false ones may be tolerable, and that a false discovery proportion may then be more desirable' (locator p. 14). The RFS text on p. 14, section 3.3.1 (round-21 read of the published PDF; carried), says that when R is large 'N0|r is no longer a suitable measure; a certain false discovery proportion may be more desirable'. So the source supports 'no longer a suitable measure', not the unqualified 'is the wrong target'. BUILDER_RULES 2.3 ('state what the paper shows ... never generalize') and 5 (a contested B claim names its counter-evidence) are not met by the headline. Counter-evidence search (row L01-L02-counter-screen-0f4068a): JKP (2023) and Chen (2021, 2025) contest HLZ's conclusions, not this remark; Chen (2025) says FDR-type statistics are strongly identified from published findings, which supports an FDP target; the registry's Lehmann and Romano (2005) k-FWER (key lehmann2005generalizations) is the published middle ground between FWER and FDP and would be the natural citation for the headline's scope. No named source contests the FWER remark itself.
rows.fix: In course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 345, replace 'FWER is the wrong target when discoveries are many.' with 'Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue that, when the total number of discoveries is large, the family-wise error rate is no longer a suitable measure.' (the attribution is to HLZ's p. 14 text; the builder should read p. 14 once to confirm that 'N0|r' there refers to the family-wise error rate, which the same section defines as P(N0|r > 0)). The next sentence keeps its own B span. Then run check_pages --unit S7 --page L02 and page_smoke --unit S7 --pages L02.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L01.html line 436 (Lab 4 interpretation: 'The price of validity is time.'); Remark 6.9 (line 454, 'Its price is the wider boundary') is scoped by the monitor's definition and needs no change
rows.evidence: The sentence is a general, ungraded claim about anytime-valid inference, and a named published 2026 result contests it as a general statement. Koning and van Meer (2026), 'Anytime validity is free: inducing sequential tests', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, issued 21 February 2026, DOI 10.1093/jrsssb/qkag050 (Crossref record read at 0f4068a; r22/downloads/counter_ramdas_abstracts_r22.json): 'Given a maximum number of observations N, one may believe this must come at the cost of power when compared to a conventional test that waits until all N observations have arrived. Our first contribution is to show that this is false: for any valid test based on N observations, we show how to construct an anytime valid sequential test that matches it after N observations.' The page's sentence is true for the monitor of Proposition 6.6, which is valid at every horizon with no known N (the price there is the wider boundary and the time to detection, Example 6.7 and Lab 4), but 'the price of validity is time' is stated as a property of validity. For a known maximum horizon the 2026 result removes the power cost at that horizon. The DOI is not in references/references.json (checked by grep of the registry for the DOI: no entry). Freshness (VERIFIER_RULES 2.1): this is 2026 work for any debate brief on anytime-valid inference. Counter-screen: row L01-L02-counter-screen-0f4068a (the 68 citing DOIs of Ramdas et al. 2023 screened at 0f4068a: this paper and Safe testing are the items on the price of anytime validity).
rows.fix: (1) Add the registry entry for DOI 10.1093/jrsssb/qkag050 with tools/add_reference.py (proposed key koning2026anytime; the add tool checks the Crossref record). (2) In course/modules/S/S7/L01.html line 436, replace 'The price of validity is time.' with 'For a monitor that must stay valid at every horizon, the price is time.' (3) In the same paragraph, after that sentence, insert: 'With a known maximum number of observations N, Koning and van Meer show that an anytime-valid sequential test can match a fixed-N test after N observations, so the cost is not inevitable.' (grade B and the locator 'Abstract' are what the published abstract supports; a theorem locator may replace them after the paper is read). (4) Run check_pages --unit S7 --page L01 and page_smoke --unit S7 --pages L01.

Read in full (abstracts): Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen (2023, J. Read by title only: 'A Critique of Size-Related Anomalies' (RFS 1995; anomalies, not the size of sorted-portfolio tests); 'Is Momentum Due to Data-snooping?' (EJF 2007; no abstract); 'Quantifying Backtest Overfitting in Alternative Beta Strategies' (JPM 2017; no abstract); 'Four Problems With Group Sequential Methods' (Whitehead 1991; letter, no abstract). Result: no named published source contests the four HLZ spans, the Lo-MacKinlay size statement, the White single-history statement, the Romano-Wolf comparison, the O'Brien-Fleming size-and-power finding, the Johari deployment report or the Ramdas/Wang/Howard definitions and theorems. The HLZ conclusions (replication, hurdles) are contested by JKP (2023) and Chen (2021, 2025); the page does not assert them, so the spans stand.
